mainEntity.name: How do I know if my filling is too large and needs a crown?

acceptedAnswer.text: Your dentist is well placed to assess this during a clinical examination. However, signs that may suggest a filling has become problematic include sensitivity to temperature, discomfort when chewing, visible cracks around the filling, or the filling appearing raised or discoloured. In many cases, a dentist may identify concerns during a routine check-up using X-rays before any symptoms develop. If you have a large or old filling, attending regular check-ups is a reliable way to monitor its condition over time.

mainEntity.name: Can a tooth with a large filling still be saved with a crown?

acceptedAnswer.text: In many cases, yes — a crown can be used to restore and protect a tooth with a large filling, provided there is sufficient natural tooth structure remaining and the pulp of the tooth is healthy. If decay has reached the pulp, root canal treatment may be needed first. Your dentist will assess the overall health of the tooth, including the bone and surrounding gum tissue, before recommending a course of treatment. Individual outcomes depend on the specific clinical picture at the time of examination.

mainEntity.name: How long does a dental crown last?

acceptedAnswer.text: Dental crowns are durable restorations, but they are not permanent in the same way as natural teeth. With good oral hygiene and regular dental check-ups, a crown may last for many years. The longevity of a crown can be influenced by factors such as the material used, the position of the tooth, biting habits, and how well the tooth and crown are maintained. Your dentist will advise on the specific material recommended for your situation and what you can do to help extend its lifespan.

mainEntity.name: Does getting a dental crown hurt?

acceptedAnswer.text: The procedure to prepare and fit a crown is typically carried out under local anaesthesia, so discomfort during the procedure is minimised. Some patients experience mild sensitivity around the prepared tooth between appointments, particularly with a temporary crown in place. After the permanent crown is fitted, any initial sensitivity usually settles within a short period. If you experience prolonged or significant discomfort following treatment, it is advisable to contact your dental practice so they can assess the situation.

mainEntity.name: Is it possible to have decay under a crown?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, decay can develop at the margin where the crown meets the natural tooth, particularly if oral hygiene in that area is not maintained. This is sometimes referred to as secondary or recurrent decay. Thorough brushing, cleaning between teeth, and attending regular check-ups help reduce this risk. If decay does develop beneath a crown, it may mean the crown needs to be removed and the tooth reassessed. This underlines the importance of good ongoing dental care, even with a crown in place.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between a crown and a large filling?

acceptedAnswer.text: A large filling replaces the missing tooth structure within the tooth, while leaving the outer walls of the natural tooth intact. A crown fits over the entire visible portion of the tooth above the gumline, acting as a protective cap. When the walls of natural tooth remaining around a large filling are thin or weakened, a crown can offer a greater degree of protection against fracture and may help extend the long-term viability of the tooth. The choice between a filling and a crown depends on individual clinical factors assessed by your dentist.
